https://www.indiablooms.com/health/lakes.text: Health Lakes and rivers may look clean, but new study finds hidden health risks People swimming in rivers and lakes could be putting themselves at risk of nasty skin conditions and stomach bugs, according to a new study from the University of East Anglia. Researchers found that people who swam in rivers and lakes were more than twice as likely to develop skin problems, while higher levels of bacteria linked to faecal pollution were associated with an increased risk of stomach bugs, reads the University of East Anglia. website. The findings come amid growing public concern over water quality and a boom in open-water swimming. How the research happened The research was conducted by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Health Protection Research Unit in Gastrointestinal Infections at UEA. Scientists analysed data from 2,368 volunteers who took part in a rare randomised controlled trial at four freshwater bathing sites in Hungary. Participants were randomly assigned either to spend 10 minutes swimming, including at least three full head immersions, or to remain on the shore without entering the water. Prof Paul Hunter, from UEA’s Norwich Medical School, led the analysis. He said: “We found that swimmers were more than twice as likely to suffer skin ailments such as rashes, ulcers or itching compared with those who stayed dry. “We also found that the risk of gastrointestinal illness increased as levels of E. coli and viruses that infect bacteria found in the human gut rose in the water, which is indicative of faecal pollution. “This work provides some of the strongest evidence yet that contamination in freshwater recreational sites can translate into real-world illness among bathers." The hidden dangers in seemingly clean water Although all four study sites met European bathing water standards at the time of the trial, scientists still detected an association between higher levels of microbial contamination and sickness. The study found that for each tenfold increase in E. coli concentration, the risk of gastrointestinal illness rose by around 73 per cent, while higher levels of viruses known as somatic coliphages were associated with a 45 per cent increase in risk. The team say these organisms appear to be better indicators of illness risk in rivers and lakes than intestinal enterococci – a bacteria group currently emphasised in some international water-quality guidance. They also noted that freshwater and coastal waters may require different standards as the behaviour of bacterial indicators differs between the two environments. Swimmers itch One intriguing finding was that skin complaints increased among swimmers regardless of measured levels of faecal indicators. “This could be due to exposure to naturally occurring organisms not linked to sewage pollution,” said Prof Hunter. “One possibility is cercarial dermatitis, commonly known as ‘swimmer's itch’, which is caused by parasites shed by waterfowl that can penetrate human skin and trigger an itchy rash. “Agricultural or industrial contaminants may also play a role,” he added. Growing relevance for UK swimmers The findings add fuel to the debate over the condition of Britain's rivers and lakes. Open-water swimming has surged in popularity in recent years, with advocates praising the mental and physical health benefits of spending time in natural ‘blue spaces’. But campaigners have repeatedly raised concerns about sewage discharges and pollution affecting popular bathing locations. “Our results were consistent across the four Hungarian study sites, which differed in water quality and water types. Our results were also consistent with a previous study in Germany. So overall, this suggests that the relationships that we have identified are generalisable and likely applicable in UK waters,” said Prof Hunter. “But it is important to remember that the rates of illness were relatively low overall and most illnesses were mild and short lived,” he added. “Just over two per cent of participants developed gastrointestinal illness and a similar proportion experienced skin ailments. Respiratory, ear and eye infections were rare.” Nevertheless, the team concluded that higher concentrations of E. coli and related indicators were clearly associated with greater risks of stomach illness, providing evidence that monitoring these microbes remains important for protecting public health. This project was a collaboration of partners from several European institutions, known as Epibathe. The Epibathe projects investigated the risks associated with both marine and freshwater sites. Hungary was chosen for the inland water studies because of the availability of good study sites and experienced local researchers. This final analysis was led by the University of East Anglia. This study was funded by the EU’s 6th Research Framework Programme, and by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Health Protection Research Unit in Gastrointestinal Infections, a partnership between the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and the University of East Anglia. https://www.rte.ie/news/business/2026/10.text: Updated / Friday, 30 Oct 2026 12:47 Getty Temu's owner PDD Holdings said in August new fee would have a considerable impact on parts of the business European Union charges on cheap e-commerce packages entering the bloc, which target Chinese platforms such as Shein and Temu, could raise €6 billion a year for the EU budget from 2028 to 2034, a Commission document seen by Reuters today showed. The estimate, previously unreported, shows the scale of Europe's crackdown on a flood of cheap ecommerce imports, which it says mostly come from China. Some 5.8 billion parcels worth less than €150 entered the EU last year, a 26% rise from the previous year, according to the European Commission, which estimates the majority were undervalued to avoid customs duties. The EU will impose an additional €2 fee on cheap parcels on November 1, raising the charge per separate item further after a €3 charge has been imposed since the start of July. Temu's owner PDD Holdings said in August that the move would have a considerable impact on parts of the business, without quantifying it. Shein makes about a third of its revenue in Europe, and its sales in the region had already fallen before the fees were imposed, as it raised prices and cut ad spending. A European Commission spokesperson declined to comment on the revenue estimate. In a briefing with reporters today, a separate Commission official said they could not prejudge the ecommerce revenue. Dirk Gotink, the European Parliament lawmaker leading the bloc's customs reforms, said the new €2 fee was to tackle "a highly toxic business model of low value non-compliant e-commerce imports from China". "The newly generated revenue gives us the chance and means to reverse decades of underinvestment and to give Europe's customs authorities the resources they need to effectively protect our single market," he said. The estimate accounts for an expected decline in the numbers of low-value parcels entering the EU as Brussels expects retailers to adjust to the measures. Fees squeeze Chinese platforms The EU fees follow similar moves by the US last year to scrap duty-free treatment of online orders to address concerns over unfair competition and unsafe products. The Commission estimates some 90% of the fees collected will go into EU coffers and 10% to member states, but that could change if member states push to keep more of the proceeds, with negotiations over the 2028-2034 budget ongoing. Currently, EU member states keep 25% of the fees. Chinese ecommerce groups have already begun adapting. AliExpress, owned by Chinese ecommerce giant Alibaba, said it was increasing local warehousing in response to the fees, but warned the charges would hurt low-income households in Europe and "exacerbate the cost-of-living crisis". Temu has been offering some shoppers a discount on the fees, according to screenshots seen by Reuters, highlighting the pressure to limit sticker shock for consumers used to ordering €3 jewellery and €5 dresses. Temu did not respond to a request for comment. Newly listed Shein, which is expanding warehouse space in Poland, said it was focused on keeping prices "competitive" alongside faster and more convenient delivery. US rival Amazon said 97% of the products it sells in the EU are fulfilled from warehouses in the bloc, so very few shipments are impacted by the fees.
